title: Coupled-cluster molecular properties across the main group that extrapolate beyond training size
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables; SI available upon request
summary: Coupled-cluster theory defines the accuracy standard for molecular electronic-structure properties but scales too steeply for routine application, whereas density-functional theory is affordable yet systematically biased. We resolve this trade-off with a single equivariant network, MEHnet-MG, that predicts an effective one-electron Hamiltonian from one inexpensive B3LYP/def2-SVP calculation and derives a broad suite of properties from it (energy, optical gap, dipole, quadrupole, polarizability, Mulliken atomic charges, and Mayer bond orders) at coupled-cluster accuracy across nine main-group elements, including the under-served phosphorus, sulfur, and chlorine chemistries. The model is trained on a new in-house dataset of multi-property labels computed at the CCSD(T) level for all nine elements. On a held-out test set, it reduces the error of every property by a factor of 3.8 to 230 relative to semi-local, hybrid, and double-hybrid DFT (referenced to composite CCSD(T)/cc-pVTZ; Methods), while adding only ~25 ms wall time per molecule, delivering coupled-cluster-quality predictions at the cost of a single DFT calculation. Critically, deriving every property from a predicted Hamiltonian rather than pooling per-atom features builds the correct size-scaling into the model architecture: on pi-conjugated oligothiophenes it matches finite-field CCSD polarizability and the EOM-CCSD optical gap to ~2% at the largest sizes where those references remain affordable (44 and 37 atoms, where a single CCSD field point already costs ~500x the model's entire inference) and extrapolates the corrected trends to 58-atom chains, a regime where pooling-based architectures fail by construction. Accurate extrapolation is therefore set by the model's inductive bias rather than by the training data.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MEHnet-MG, a single equivariant neural network that predicts an effective one-electron Hamiltonian from an inexpensive B3LYP/def2-SVP calculation and derives multiple molecular properties (energy, optical gap, dipole, quadrupole, polarizability, Mulliken charges, Mayer bond orders) at CCSD(T) coupled-cluster accuracy across nine main-group elements, reducing errors by 3.8–230× relative to various DFT functionals while adding only ~25 ms wall time per molecule. Because properties are derived from a predicted Hamiltonian rather than per-atom feature pooling, the architecture correctly builds size-scaling into the model, enabling accurate extrapolation to molecules larger than those in the training set where pooling-based methods fail.
AI.motivation: Coupled-cluster theory is the accuracy standard for molecular electronic structure but scales too steeply for routine use, while density-functional theory is affordable yet systematically biased. The authors aim to resolve this accuracy/cost trade-off with a single model that delivers coupled-cluster-quality predictions at the cost of a single DFT calculation.
AI.method: MEHnet-MG is a single equivariant network that takes as input one inexpensive B3LYP/def2-SVP calculation and predicts an effective one-electron Hamiltonian, from which a broad suite of properties is derived. It is trained on a new in-house dataset of multi-property labels computed at the CCSD(T) level covering nine main-group elements including phosphorus, sulfur, and chlorine. The Hamiltonian-based design (rather than pooling per-atom features) builds correct size-scaling into the architecture.
AI.result: On a held-out test set, the model reduces the error of every property by a factor of 3.8 to 230 relative to semi-local, hybrid, and double-hybrid DFT (referenced to composite CCSD(T)/cc-pVTZ), while adding only ~25 ms wall time per molecule. On pi-conjugated oligothiophenes it matches finite-field CCSD polarizability and EOM-CCSD optical gap to ~2% at the largest trainable reference sizes (44 and 37 atoms), where a single CCSD field point costs ~500× the model's entire inference, and extrapolates corrected trends to 58-atom chains where pooling-based architectures fail by construction.
AI.conclusion: Deriving every property from a predicted Hamiltonian rather than pooling per-atom features is critical for building correct size-scaling into the model architecture. Accurate extrapolation is therefore set by the model's inductive bias rather than by the training data, enabling coupled-cluster-quality predictions beyond the regime where coupled-cluster references remain affordable.

title: Science Done on a Machine by a Machine: AI Agents in Computational Chemistry
summary: We are witnessing an explosion of agentic systems for computational chemistry simulations: from half a dozen in 2024 to a dozen in 2025, and the current number approaches fifty, surveyed in this Perspective as of 8 August 2026. The capabilities of these agentic systems are shifting from assisting in performing a selection of computational tasks to autonomous design and execution of \textit{in silico} experiments, their analysis, and even manuscript writing. The ultimate destination is a fully autonomous AI scientist, where the entirety of computational chemistry is performed on a machine by a machine, without human supervision. While we are not there yet, and all reported systems currently involve a human in the loop, the trend is unmistakable. Even building specialized agentic systems for computational chemistry is increasingly commoditized by generalist agents, which may in the end replace the need for the specialized ones altogether, since adding a new capability will be as easy as asking AI to do it for you. Both the explosion in their number and the very limited adoption beyond their own developers point that way, and we close this Perspective on what it leaves us to do. The speed and scale of disruption agentic systems are bringing to computational chemistry leave many of us dumbfounded about the field's future and what we should spend our efforts on, as already established specialists, teachers, and students, and we have no answer.

AI.tldr: This Perspective surveys the explosive growth of agentic AI systems for computational chemistry, documenting their rise from half a dozen in 2024 to nearly fifty by August 2026. The systems are evolving from task-assisting tools toward autonomous design and execution of in silico experiments and manuscript writing, with the ultimate goal being a fully autonomous AI scientist. Despite current human-in-the-loop requirements, the trend toward complete automation and commoditization of specialized systems by generalist agents is unmistakable, raising profound questions about the field's future for researchers, teachers, and students.
AI.motivation: The rapid proliferation of agentic systems for computational chemistry—from ~6 in 2024 to ~50 in 2026—creates uncertainty about the field's future direction. The authors aim to survey the landscape and provoke discussion about what this disruption means for established specialists, teachers, and students who face an uncertain professional future.
AI.method: The paper is a Perspective (survey/review) that catalogues and analyzes the emerging range of agentic AI systems for computational chemistry, tracking their growth, capability shifts (from task assistance to autonomous experiment design/execution and manuscript writing), and the trend toward commoditization by generalist agents.
AI.result: As of 8 August 2026, nearly fifty agentic systems exist for computational chemistry. They are shifting from selection of computational tasks toward autonomous in silico experiment design, execution, analysis, and manuscript writing. However, all reported systems still require a human in the loop. The authors observe that specialized systems are increasingly being commoditized by generalist agents, which may eventually replace them entirely, evidenced by both the explosive growth in system numbers and limited adoption beyond developers.
AI.conclusion: The trajectory is unmistakable toward fully autonomous AI scientists, though that point is not yet reached. The commoditization trend suggests building specialized systems may become obsolete as generalist agents can be instructed to perform new capabilities. The authors conclude without an answer to the field's future, leaving the community with open questions about what practitioners should focus their efforts on amid this disruption.

title: UBio-MolFM: Enabling Biomolecular Dynamics at DFT Accuracy and $10^5$ Atoms with One Untuned Potential
summary: Ion conduction, membrane permeation and metal recognition hinge on electronic structure, yet first-principles simulation reaches only hundreds of atoms. UBio-MolFM lifts that ceiling: a foundation model trained on 160 million quantum-chemical labels, its receptive field spanning non-covalent distances at near-linear cost. The barrier is cost, not principle. One untuned potential keeps force error near 20 meV/Å past a thousand atoms, reproduces water's X-ray structure and ion hydration, and holds an RNA Mg$^{2+}$ site without ion-specific parameters. Cyclosporine A pays 3.5 kcal/mol in water for its permeable conformer, gated by one kinetically asymmetric hydrogen bond that a fixed-charge model flattens. In a 108,964-atom KcsA channel on one GPU, the relaxed four-ion column is anhydrous in all five replicas, in direct contact in four---the knock-on geometry ten fixed-charge simulations never form. It remains orders of magnitude costlier. Where electronic structure decides the answer, first-principles simulation is in reach.

AI.tldr: UBio-MolFM is a foundation model trained on 160 million quantum-chemical labels that enables first-principles-quality simulation across non-covalent distances at near-linear cost. It maintains ~20 meV/Å force error beyond a thousand atoms, reproduces water X-ray structure and ion hydration, holds an RNA Mg²⁺ site without ion-specific parameters, reveals cyclosporine A's permeable conformer costs 3.5 kcal/mol gated by a kinetically asymmetric H-bond, and recovers the correct four-ion knock-on geometry in a 108,964-atom KcsA potassium channel that ten fixed-charge simulations never form.
AI.motivation: First-principles quantum-chemical simulation is limited to hundreds of atoms, creating a barrier between electronic-structure accuracy and the system sizes relevant to ion conduction, membrane permeation, and metal recognition in biology.
AI.method: A foundation model (UBio-MolFM) trained on 160 million quantum-chemical labels, with a receptive field spanning non-covalent distances at near-linear computational cost, applied as a universal (untuned) potential.
AI.result: Force error stays near 20 meV/Å beyond a thousand atoms; water's X-ray structure and ion hydration are reproduced; an RNA Mg²⁺ site is stable without ion-specific parameters; cyclosporine A's permeable conformer costs 3.5 kcal/mol in water with one kinetically asymmetric H-bond flattened by fixed-charge models; a 108,964-atom KcsA channel on one GPU relaxes to an anhydrous four-ion column in all five replicas with direct ion-ion contact in four, forming a knock-on geometry never observed in ten fixed-charge simulations.
AI.conclusion: While UBio-MolFM remains orders of magnitude costlier than classical potentials, it makes first-principles simulation reachable at biologically relevant scales wherever electronic structure determines the answer.

title: Molecular Insights into Gas Nanofilms Confined Between Bulk Liquid Phases
summary: Nanometer-thick fluid films play a critical role in confined multiphase processes, yet the thermodynamics and stability of free gas nanofilms remain poorly understood compared with their liquid counterparts. Here, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are employed to systematically investigate gas nanofilms confined between bulk liquid phases using Lennard-Jones argon as a model system. The results show that the surface tension decreases exponentially with decreasing film thickness, accompanied by an increasing magnitude of the negative disjoining pressure. Upon thinning, the planar gas film undergoes a distinct morphological transition from a stable planar state to a transient or persistent spherical bubble through the formation and growth of a liquid bridge. The film surface area strongly affects its thermodynamic properties, with larger areas producing stronger thickness dependence and larger deviations from classical density functional theory (cDFT) predictions. The closer agreement between MD and cDFT at smaller surface areas suggests that the discrepancy primarily arises from thermal capillary-wave fluctuations, which are included in MD but omitted in mean-field cDFT. Moreover, at small film thicknesses, the magnitude of the disjoining pressure increases with decreasing temperature, consistent with the enhanced sensitivity of the confined gas phase to thickness variations and contrasting with the trend generally reported for liquid nanofilms. These findings provide molecular insights into the thermodynamics and stability of gas nanofilms, with implications for confined multiphase transport and droplet coalescence.

AI.tldr: This paper uses molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with Lennard-Jones argon to investigate the thermodynamics and stability of gas nanofilms confined between bulk liquid phases. The surface tension decreases exponentially with film thickness, accompanied by negative disjoining pressure. Films undergo morphological transitions from planar to spherical bubble states via liquid bridge formation. Deviations from classical density functional theory arise from thermal capillary-wave fluctuations, and the disjoining pressure increases in magnitude with decreasing temperature at small thicknesses.
AI.motivation: While confined liquid nanofilms have been extensively studied, the thermodynamics and stability of free gas nanofilms (gas films trapped between bulk liquids) remain poorly understood, despite their critical role in confined multiphase processes such as transport and droplet coalescence.
AI.method: Systematic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using Lennard-Jones argon as a model system to investigate gas nanofilms confined between bulk liquid phases, with parametric variation of film thickness, surface area, and temperature. Results are compared against classical density functional theory (cDFT) predictions.
AI.result: (1) Surface tension decreases exponentially with decreasing film thickness with increasing negative disjoining pressure; (2) planar gas films transition to transient or persistent spherical bubbles via liquid bridge formation and growth; (3) larger film surface areas produce stronger thickness dependence and larger deviations from cDFT due to thermal capillary-wave fluctuations; (4) at small thicknesses, disjoining pressure magnitude increases with decreasing temperature, opposite to the trend for liquid nanofilms.
AI.conclusion: The study provides molecular-level insights into gas nanofilm thermodynamics and stability, identifying capillary-wave fluctuations as the primary source of MD-cDFT discrepancy and revealing distinct temperature behavior compared to liquid nanofilms. These findings have implications for understanding confined multiphase transport and droplet coalescence phenomena.

title: Learning constructive models of emergent systems
comment: Supplemental Table pertaining to the chorismate mutase assay and experimental results can be found in the associated github repository mentioned in the paper
summary: Emergent systems - systems containing multi-scale interactions - often arise through iteration rather than explicit forward design. As such, design principles for building emergent systems have been under-explored. Current artificial intelligence architectures, while useful for generation, do not provide a logic for how to construct emergent systems. Inspired by statistical phylogenetics, we show that inferring scales of system entropy then explicitly constraining information flow from low to high entropic scales yields data-driven, stepwise 'constructive models' of emergent systems. We term the resulting architecture the Layer-Restricted Boltzmann Machine (LRBM). Applied identically to digit images, natural language, and enzyme sequences, LRBM models follow hierarchical logic: lower layers encode global structure from which higher layers encode fine-grained features. As a stringent experimental challenge for LRBM-based construction, we built and evaluated 160 constructive trajectories of synthetic and 1,130 natural chorismate mutase (CM) enzymes in an in vivo functional assay. Designed CMs functioned up to 53% sequence divergent from the nearest natural homolog. Notably, enzyme fold emerged at intermediate LRBM layers while function arose only upon satisfying all layers. Fold was therefore necessary but insufficient for function in this enzyme family. Our results suggest a shared hierarchical, learnable statistical logic for constructing emergent systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Layer-Restricted Boltzmann Machine (LRBM), an architecture inspired by statistical phylogenetics that infers scales of system entropy and constrains information flow from low to high entropic scales to construct emergent systems in a data-driven, stepwise manner. Applied across digit images, natural language, and enzyme sequences, LRBMs reveal a consistent hierarchical logic where low layers encode global structure and high layers encode fine-grained features. In the challenging in vivo test with chorismate mutase enzymes, designed enzymes functioned up to 53% sequence divergence from the nearest natural homolog, and while enzyme fold emerged at intermediate layers, function only arose when all layers were satisfied—demonstrating fold is necessary but insufficient for function.
AI.motivation: Emergent systems with multi-scale interactions typically arise through iteration rather than explicit design, leaving design principles under-explored. Current AI architectures support generation but lack a logic for constructing emergent systems, motivating a principled framework for building them.
AI.method: The authors propose inferring scales of system entropy and explicitly constraining information flow from low to high entropic scales, yielding a stepwise 'constructive model' architecture termed the Layer-Restricted Boltzmann Machine (LRBM). The approach is applied identically across digit images, natural language, and enzyme sequences, and validated through 160 synthetic and 1,130 natural chorismate mutase enzyme constructive trajectories tested in an in vivo functional assay.
AI.result: Designed chorismate mutase enzymes functioned up to 53% sequence divergence from the nearest natural homolog. Enzyme fold emerged at intermediate LRBM layers, whereas function arose only when all layers were satisfied, demonstrating that fold is necessary but insufficient for function in this enzyme family.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest a shared hierarchical, learnable statistical logic for constructing emergent systems, indicating that principled design of emergent systems is achievable through entropy-scale-aware information-flow constraints.

title: Embedding Paired Free-Fermion Gaussian States into Gutzwiller-Projected Bardeen--Cooper--Schrieffer Wave Functions
comment: 2 pages, 1 figure. All codes and data used in this manuscript are available at https://github.com/ryuikaneko/mvmc_1d_transverse_field_ising
summary: Gutzwiller-projected Bardeen--Cooper--Schrieffer (BCS) wave functions of Abrikosov fermions are widely used to describe quantum many-body states. Taking the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model as an example, we exactly embed any even-parity spinless fermionic Gaussian state representable as a paired exponential in the chosen particle basis into a projected BCS state of spinful Abrikosov fermions. The construction provides controlled initial states for variational Monte Carlo studies of nonintegrable models.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that any even-parity spinless fermionic Gaussian state (representable as a paired exponential) can be exactly embedded into a Gutzwiller-projected BCS wave function of spinful Abrikosov fermions, using the 1D transverse-field Ising model as a concrete example. This provides controlled initial states for variational Monte Carlo simulations of nonintegrable models.
AI.motivation: Gutzwiller-projected BCS wave functions of Abrikosov fermions are widely used but a systematic, exact embedding of arbitrary fermionic Gaussian states into this framework was lacking, limiting their use as controlled initial states in variational Monte Carlo studies of nonintegrable systems.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate an exact construction that embeds any even-parity spinless fermionic Gaussian state—expressible as a paired exponential in the chosen particle basis—into a projected BCS state of spinful Abrikosov fermions. The 1D transverse-field Ising model is used as an illustrative example of the construction.
AI.result: The construction provides an exact embedding of even-parity spinless fermionic Gaussian states into projective BCS wave functions, yielding controlled initial states for variational Monte Carlo studies of nonintegrable models, as exemplified in the 1D transverse-field Ising model.
AI.conclusion: This exact embedding framework enables broader and more controlled applications of projected BCS wave functions in variational Monte Carlo simulations of nonintegrable quantum many-body systems.

title: Engineering kekule superconductivity from layer-selective interactions in rhombohedral graphene
summary: At weak coupling, finite-momentum superconductivity is typically associated with broken time-reversal or inversion symmetry of the Fermi surface. Here, we show that lattice-scale pair-density-wave order in rhombohedral multilayer graphene can arise from layer/orbital-dependent pairing interactions, band chirality, and Dirac-point-centered Fermi surface topology while preserving both symmetries. Using mean-field theory and comparing finite momentum sectors $Q = \pm 2 K_{D}$ with the $ Q = 0$ superconducting state, we find that layer-dependent interactions of opposite signs ($V_{1A}=-V_{JB}=-|V|$) favor an intra-valley Kekulè state with center-of-mass momentum ($ Q=\pm 2 K_D$). In the presence of a time-reversal and inversion symmetry-preserving Kane-Mele mass ($λ$), this state appears only above a critical carrier density ($n^{crit}_{K}(λ,J)$). The two superconducting condensates exhibit opposite chirality, $J(-J)$ for $K_D(-K_D) $ valleys, thereby preserving time-reversal and inversion symmetry. We map the phase diagram and analyze the dependence of $T_c$ on the chirality index $J$ and $λ$. We also evaluate the superfluid stiffness in the Kekulè superconducting state, thereby determining the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition temperature. Our results show that orbital-dependent interactions in the presence of band chirality favor finite-momentum pairing in time-reversal and inversion symmetric Dirac materials.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that finite-momentum (Kekulè) superconductivity in rhombohedral multilayer graphene can arise from layer/orbital-dependent pairing interactions without breaking time-reversal or inversion symmetry, with the superconducting condensates exhibiting opposite chirality in opposite valleys.
AI.motivation: Finite-momentum superconductivity is typically thought to require broken time-reversal or inversion symmetry at weak coupling. The authors investigate whether lattice-scale pair-density-wave order can exist in rhombohedral multilayer graphene while preserving both symmetries, expanding the understanding of when finite-momentum pairing is possible.
AI.method: The authors use mean-field theory to compare finite-momentum sectors Q = ±2K_D with the Q = 0 superconducting state. They consider layer-dependent pairing interactions of opposite signs (V_{1A} = -V_{JB} = -|V|) and a Kane-Mele mass λ that preserves both time-reversal and inversion symmetry. They map the phase diagram, analyze the T_c dependence on chirality index J and λ, and compute the superfluid stiffness to determine the BKT transition temperature.
AI.result: Layer-dependent interactions of opposite signs favor an intra-valley Kekulè state with center-of-mass momentum Q = ±2K_D. This state appears only above a critical carrier density n^crit_K(λ,J) in the presence of the Kane-Mele mass. The two superconducting condensates have opposite chirality (J for K_D and -J for -K_D valleys), preserving both time-reversal and inversion symmetry. The paper provides the full phase diagram, T_c dependence on J and λ, and BKT transition temperatures from superfluid stiffness calculations.
AI.conclusion: Orbital-dependent interactions combined with band chirality and Dirac-point-centered Fermi surface topology can favor finite-momentum pairing in time-reversal and inversion symmetric Dirac materials, extending the paradigm of when pair-density-wave order can arise at weak coupling.

title: Probing the electroweak structure of nuclei with rare atoms and molecules
summary: Precision experiments of atoms and molecules have become a powerful probe of the electroweak structure of atomic nuclei and of physics beyond the Standard Model. We review how the interaction between a nucleus and its surrounding bound electrons can be exploited to precisely measure the electromagnetic, parity-violating, and CP-violating properties of nuclei and their fundamental constituents. We focus on rare, unstable isotopes, surveying the experimental techniques and facilities developed in recent years that have extended these measurements to the most exotic regions of the nuclear chart. Recent advances in the precision control and interrogation of single molecules, together with direct laser excitation of nuclear transitions, are opening new frontiers in nuclear and particle physics. At the same time, progress in nuclear theory, machine learning, and high-performance computing is strengthening the connection between our microscopic description of nature and laboratory observables. In many cases, the precision with which nuclear and particle physics properties can be extracted is now limited not by experiment, but by the molecular, atomic, or nuclear theory required to interpret the measurements. This challenge presents a major opportunity for combined theoretical and experimental advances that will enable future discoveries.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews how precision measurements of atoms and molecules probe the electroweak structure of nuclei and physics beyond the Standard Model, focusing on rare, unstable isotopes and surveying recent experimental techniques, facilities, theoretical advances, and future opportunities at the frontier of nuclear and particle physics.
AI.motivation: Precision experiments on atoms and molecules have emerged as a powerful tool to probe the electroweak structure of atomic nuclei and search for physics beyond the Standard Model. The review aims to consolidate how nuclear-electron interactions enable precise measurements of electromagnetic, parity-violating, and CP-violating properties of nuclei, with particular focus on extending these measurements to rare, unstable isotopes across the nuclear chart.
AI.method: The paper reviews experimental techniques and facilities developed in recent years for precision atomic and molecular measurements on exotic nuclei, including single-molecule precision control and interrogation, and direct laser excitation of nuclear transitions. It also surveys theoretical advances in nuclear theory, machine learning, and high-performance computing that connect microscopic descriptions of nature to laboratory observables.
AI.result: The paper finds that precision extraction of nuclear and particle physics properties is now often limited not by experimental capability but by the molecular, atomic, or nuclear theory required to interpret measurements. This represents a paradigm shift where theoretical understanding has become the bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: The current theory-limited regime presents a major opportunity for combined theoretical and experimental advances that could enable future discoveries in nuclear and particle physics, particularly through precision measurements on rare, unstable isotopes.

title: On the electronic and vibrational dimensionality of nanometer-scale silicon structures
summary: We discuss the problem of assessing the electronic and vibrational dimensionality of a semiconductor nanostructure: How thin and/or wide must a nanostructure be in order to induce electron and phonon confinement? Clarifying the physical justification for common criteria found in the literature, we view the electron coherence length (defined as the electron and phonon inelastic mean free path) as their `field of view' and argue (or, better yet, `speculate') that this sets the important length scale. Considering the example of Si nanosheets at room temperature, and drawing from results found in the literature, we estimate that the critical length below which electrons are subject to quantum confinement is of the order of (or smaller than) 8 nm, when their coherence length is determined by energy losses to phonons and remote phonons in gated structures. On the contrary, no single length-scale can be given for phonons: Taking their coherence length as determined by scattering with electrons and anharmonic three-phonon processes, short wavelength acoustic and optical phonons may be confined only by structures as small as 10 nm. Long-wavelength acoustic phonons, instead, may exhibit a coherence length of the order of 1 micrometer, so that they may be confined over much larger distances.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses how thin/wide a semiconductor nanostructure must be to induce electron and phonon confinement, proposing that the electron/phonon inelastic mean free path (coherence length) is the key length scale. For Si nanosheets at room temperature, electron quantum confinement occurs below ~8 nm (limited by phonon and remote-phonon scattering), while phonon confinement has no single length scale: short-wavelength acoustic/optical phonons confine only below ~10 nm, but long-wavelength acoustic phonons can be confined over ~1 micrometer distances.
AI.motivation: To clarify the physical justification behind common criteria for dimensionality transitions in semiconductor nanostructures, which are often ambiguous or not physically grounded, by identifying the correct length scale that governs electron and phonon confinement.
AI.method: The authors treat the electron and phonon coherence length (inelastic mean free path) as the nanostructure's 'field of view' determining dimensionality. They compile and analyze literature data on scattering mechanisms (electron-phonon, remote-phonon in gated structures, anharmonic three-phonon processes) for Si nanosheets at room temperature to estimate critical confinement lengths for electrons and different phonon branches.
AI.result: The critical confinement length for electrons in Si nanosheets at room temperature is estimated at ~8 nm or smaller, dictated by energy losses to phonons and remote phonons. For phonons, short-wavelength acoustic and optical phonons require structures as small as ~10 nm to be confined, whereas long-wavelength acoustic phonons exhibit coherence lengths of ~1 micrometer, enabling confinement over much larger distances.
AI.conclusion: Dimensionality in semiconductor nanostructures is governed by the quasiparticle coherence length rather than a single geometric factor. Electron confinement is characterized by a single critical scale (~8 nm for Si), but phonon confinement is wavelength-dependent, ranging from ~10 nm for short-wavelength modes to ~1 micrometer for long-wavelength acoustic phonons, making a unified phonon dimensionality criterion impossible.

title: Chern insulator boundary criticality
summary: We investigate signatures of chirality at Chern insulator transitions in the presence of a boundary. The transition between a trivial insulator and a Chern insulator with Chern number $C=1$ is described by a massless Dirac fermion whose parity anomaly gives a critical Hall conductivity $σ_{xy}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{e^2}{h}$. Using a Dirac mass domain wall construction, we show that the chiral edge mode delocalizes into the bulk at criticality, but the boundary fermion correlation function retains a chiral structure and acquires the scaling dimension of the bulk fermion. We compute current correlation functions and demonstrate that the anomaly of the bulk Hall response is matched by delocalized chiral modes near the boundary. Using only the residual conformal symmetry of a (2+1)d conformal field theory (CFT) in a half-space, we identify parity-odd terms in current and energy-momentum tensor correlation functions that encode these modes and determine their electromagnetic and gravitational anomaly coefficients. Our analysis therefore applies to general time-reversal breaking (2+1)d CFTs, beyond the free Dirac transition. We also extend our results to higher Chern number transitions and to the transition between a (3+1)d topological insulator and a trivial insulator.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates chirality signatures at Chern insulator transitions with boundaries, showing that chiral edge modes delocalize into the bulk at criticality while boundary fermion correlation functions retain chiral structure with bulk fermion scaling dimension. Using conformal symmetry in half-space, the authors identify parity-odd terms in current and energy-momentum tensor correlation functions that encode delocalized chiral modes and determine their electromagnetic and gravitational anomaly coefficients, extending results to general (2+1)d CFTs, higher Chern number transitions, and (3+1)d topological insulator transitions.
AI.motivation: To understand how chirality manifests at Chern insulator quantum critical points in the presence of boundaries, and to characterize the anomalous properties at the bulk-edge correspondence at criticality using conformal field theory tools.
AI.method: The authors use a Dirac mass domain wall construction and exploit the residual conformal symmetry of a (2+1)d CFT in a half-space. They compute current and energy-momentum tensor correlation functions, identifying parity-odd terms that encode delocalized chiral modes near the boundary, and extract electromagnetic and gravitational anomaly coefficients.
AI.result: They show that the chiral edge mode delocalizes into the bulk at criticality, boundary fermion correlation functions retain chiral structure with bulk fermion scaling dimension, the bulk Hall response anomaly is matched by delocalized chiral boundary modes, and the analysis applies to general time-reversal breaking (2+1)d CFTs beyond the free Dirac transition, including higher Chern number and (3+1)d topological insulator transitions.
AI.conclusion: Chirality signatures at Chern insulator transitions can be characterized universally via conformal symmetry in half-space, providing anomaly coefficients that generalize beyond the free Dirac fermion case to arbitrary (2+1)d CFTs and higher-dimensional topological insulator transitions.

title: Breaking the mutual exclusivity between metallicity and ferroelectricity in a non-polar covalent semiconductor via orbital selective doping
summary: The mutual exclusion of ferroelectricity and metallic conductivity is a long-standing tenet because itinerant electrons screen long-range Coulomb forces that stabilize the bulk polar order. Here, we break this paradigm by heavily doping a non-polar covalent semiconductor of cubic silicon carbide (3C-SiC) with nitrogen. This introduces heavy electron doping, inducing metallicity and driving a structural transition from the non-polar F-43m to the polar R3m symmetry via the pseudo-Jahn-Teller effect. Remarkably, we provide direct, atomic-scale visualization of about 180° polarization reversal under an external voltage bias in a ferroelectric metal. The strongly directional character of antibonding orbitals occupied by conduction electrons prevents them from screening the local Si-C polarization, resulting in the coexistence of metallicity and ferroelectricity. Ferroelectric tunnel junctions demonstrate nonvolatile memory properties with a well-defined high-resistance state (HRS) and low-resistance state (LRS), an ultrahigh response speed (~50 ns), an ultralow operating voltage (1 V), an endurance exceeding 85927 cycles, and a projected retention time of 100 years. Our results provide a novel strategy for pioneering ferroelectricity in a metal, a new ferroelectric metal platform for exploring exotic properties, and a ferroelectric device with high performance that meets the requirements for low consumption and high-speed non-volatile devices.

AI.tldr: This paper breaks the long-standing paradigm that ferroelectricity and metallic conductivity are mutually exclusive by heavily doping cubic silicon carbide (3C-SiC) with nitrogen. This induces metallicity and a structural transition from non-polar F-43m to polar R3m symmetry via the pseudo-Jahn-Teller effect. Atomic-scale visualization reveals ~180° polarization reversal under voltage bias in this ferroelectric metal. The directional antibonding orbitals of conduction electrons prevent screening of local Si-C polarization. Ferroelectric tunnel junctions exhibit nonvolatile memory with HRS/LRS states, ~50 ns response, 1 V operating voltage, >85927 cycles endurance, and ~100-year retention.
AI.motivation: The coexistence of ferroelectricity and metallic conductivity was long considered impossible because itinerant electrons screen the long-range Coulomb forces stabilizing bulk polar order. The authors aimed to break this paradigm and create a genuine ferroelectric metal, providing a new platform for exploring exotic physics and enabling high-performance ferroelectric devices.
AI.method: Nitrogen atoms are heavily doped into a non-polar covalent semiconductor of cubic silicon carbide (3C-SiC), introducing heavy electron doping that induces metallicity. The doping drives a structural transition from non-polar F-43m to polar R3m symmetry via the pseudo-Jahn-Teller effect. The polarization reversal was directly visualized at atomic scale under an external voltage bias, and ferroelectric tunnel junctions were fabricated to evaluate memory performance.
AI.result: Atomic-scale visualization confirmed ~180° polarization reversal under external bias in the ferroelectric metal. Ferroelectric tunnel junctions demonstrated nonvolatile memory with well-defined HRS and LRS, ultrahigh response speed (~50 ns), ultralow operating voltage (1 V), endurance exceeding 85,927 cycles, and projected retention of 100 years. The strongly directional antibonding orbitals occupied by conduction electrons prevent screening of local Si-C polarization.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a novel strategy for pioneering ferroelectricity in metals, establishing a new ferroelectric metal platform for exploring exotic properties, and delivering a high-performance ferroelectric device that meets the requirements for low-consumption, high-speed non-volatile applications.

title: Molecular Implementation of the Machine-Learned Skala Exchange-Correlation Functional in CP2K through GauXC
summary: Machine-learned exchange--correlation (XC) functionals offer a route to improve Kohn--Sham density-functional theory without incurring the cost of explicitly correlated electronic-structure methods. Their use in production simulation codes, however, requires a well-defined mapping between the learned model and the host-code density representation. We formulate and implement a Skala-1.1 interface in CP2K through the external GauXC library. CP2K supplies the geometry, Gaussian basis, spin-resolved atomic-orbital density matrix, and communicator, while GauXC evaluates the XC energy, atomic-orbital potential matrix, and available nuclear derivatives. The interface accepts both all-electron and valence-only density matrices. The latter may arise from separable dual-space pseudopotentials or molecular effective-core potentials. Implementation errors are isolated from functional differences by comparing the Perdew--Burke--Ernzerhof (PBE) functional evaluated through GauXC with native CP2K PBE. The resulting interface gives consistent energies, forces validated against finite-difference total-energy checks, and force-based molecular-virial diagnostics for representative molecular cases. The dietGMTKN55 benchmark suite is evaluated with an all-electron Gaussian augmented plane-wave treatment for elements up to bromine and def2 effective-core potentials for the heavier elements. The resulting aggregate mean absolute deviation of 1.255 kcal/mol is within 0.020 kcal/mol of the corresponding Skala reference value of 1.235 kcal/mol. This work establishes a validated molecular implementation of Skala in CP2K through GauXC.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the formulation and implementation of the Skala-1.1 machine-learned exchange-correlation functional in the CP2K simulation code through the external GauXC library, with validation against native PBE and benchmarks showing results within 0.020 kcal/mol of the Skala reference.
AI.motivation: Machine-learned XC functionals can improve Kohn-Sham DFT accuracy without the cost of correlated methods, but their practical implementation in production codes requires a well-defined mapping between the learned model and the host code's density representation. This work addresses the need for a validated molecular implementation of the Skala functional in CP2K.
AI.method: A Skala-1.1 interface is implemented in CP2K through the external GauXC library. CP2K supplies geometry, Gaussian basis, spin-resolved atomic-orbital density matrix, and communicator, while GauXC evaluates XC energy, atomic-orbital potential matrix, and nuclear derivatives. The interface supports both all-electron and valence-only density matrices (from pseudopotentials or effective-core potentials). Implementation errors are isolated from functional differences by comparing PBE through GauXC with native CP2K PBE.
AI.result: The interface yields consistent energies and forces validated against finite-difference total-energy checks and force-based molecular-virial diagnostics. The dietGMTKN55 benchmark suite, using all-electron Gaussian augmented plane-wave treatment up to bromine and def2 effective-core potentials for heavier elements, gives an aggregate mean absolute deviation of 1.255 kcal/mol, within 0.020 kcal/mol of the Skala reference value of 1.235 kcal/mol.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a validated molecular implementation of Skala in CP2K through GauXC, providing a production-ready pathway for using machine-learned exchange-correlation functionals in molecular simulation codes.

title: Topology is not silent in the transport noise of multiband bosons
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables; code and data at doi:10.5281/zenodo.21945238; companion paper: arXiv:2608.15789
summary: For electrons at a Fermi surface, the topological part of the Berry curvature drops out of the transport noise: the anomalous Hall conductivity is quantized, and the fluctuations of the Hall current know nothing about the Chern number. We show that this cancellation is an accident of the Fermi surface, and that it fails for bosons. Magnons and phonons thermally populate every band, each with its own Chern number, so the harmonic sector of the Hodge decomposition of the curvature is not a single constant and a variance does not annihilate it. What survives is the occupation-weighted dispersion of Chern numbers across populated bands. That band geometry is visible in current noise is known, and at zero temperature the antisymmetric part of the noise sum rule already returns a Chern number; what is new is an object with no zero-temperature analogue, existing only when several bands are populated and weighted differently. We derive it from a fluctuating Boltzmann equation and settle the energy-magnetization subtraction at the level of fluctuations: the subtracted term is the curl of a bounded magnetization density, so it contributes exactly zero to the current any transport measurement records, realization by realization. Is the quantity measurable? A driven protocol is not: the excess noise sits twelve orders below the equilibrium floor. An equilibrium protocol is, through a sum rule on the antisymmetric part of the current cross-spectrum, which carries no drive and hence no suppression. We prove that the frequency-integrated form of that sum rule cannot separate the topological from the geometric content, and show that the frequency-resolved cross-spectrum does separate them at accessible resolution. The protocol is specified for Cu(1,3-bdc), with its robustness to nuisance-model completeness and to dispersion, thermometry and field calibration.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that while topological Berry curvature cancels out of transport noise for fermions at the Fermi surface (an accident of Fermi statistics), it survives for bosons like magnons and phonons that thermally populate multiple bands. The authors derive a new occupation-weighted dispersion of Chern numbers across populated bands with no zero-temperature analogue, propose an equilibrium measurement protocol via the frequency-resolved antisymmetric part of the current cross-spectrum, and specify it for Cu(1,3-bdc).
AI.motivation: The authors aim to demonstrate that the cancellation of topological Berry curvature in transport noise for electrons is an artifact of the Fermi surface, and that this cancellation fails for bosons, revealing new band-geometry information not accessible at zero temperature.
AI.method: The authors derive the result from a fluctuating Boltzmann equation, resolving the energy-magnetization subtraction at the level of fluctuations (the subtracted term is the curl of a bounded magnetization density, contributing exactly zero to current transport measurements). They analyze both driven and equilibrium protocols, proving that a driven protocol fails (excess noise 12 orders below equilibrium floor) while an equilibrium protocol via the frequency-resolved antisymmetric current cross-spectrum succeeds.
AI.result: The frequency-integrated sum rule cannot separate topological from geometric content, but the frequency-resolved cross-spectrum can at accessible resolution. The protocol, specified for Cu(1,3-bdc), is robust to nuisance-model completeness, dispersion, thermometry and field calibration.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes that bosonic transport noise carries a new geometric object—the occupation-weighted dispersion of Chern numbers across populated bands—with no zero-temperature counterpart, and provides a feasible equilibrium measurement protocol for its detection.

title: Magnetism and Electrical Conduction in Lightly-Doped Single-Layer High-$T_c$ Cuprate $\mathrm{La}_2\mathrm{CuO}_{4+δ}$
summary: The temperature dependences of magnetization and electrical resistivity as well as their magnetic field dependences have been examined in lightly-doped single-layer cuprate $\mathrm{La}_2\mathrm{CuO}_{4+δ}$ (LCO, hole-doping level $p \, (2δ) \cong 0.03$) single crystals, in comparison with those in the extremely low doping region of $p \lesssim 0.015$ to uncover the intrinsic magnetism and electrical conduction of the $\mathrm{Cu\text{-}O}$ plane that exhibits both antiferromagnetic (AF) and superconducting (SC) orders simultaneously. In $p \cong 0.03$ SC LCO, the sub-lattice moments on $\mathrm{Cu}$ sites and their AF couplings are only $\sim 15\,\%$ smaller than those of the Mott-insulator parent material, suggesting that the localization of $\mathrm{Cu}$ $3d$ electrons remains very strong. Furthermore, we report that in the SC LCO, two-dimensional AF spin correlations develop rapidly from $T^* \cong 280\text{ K}$ towards Néel temperature $T_{\mathrm{N}} = 266\text{ K}$, where the out-of-plane resistivity starts to decrease largely. This might be responsible for the AF ordering at such a high temperature in the SC single-layer cuprate with $p \cong 0.03$.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates lightly-doped single-layer cuprate La2CuO4+δ (LCO) single crystals at hole-doping p≈0.03, examining magnetization and electrical resistivity vs. temperature and magnetic field, and comparing with extremely low doping (p≲0.015). It reveals that Cu-site sub-lattice moments and AF couplings remain strong (~15% smaller than the Mott-insulator parent), and that 2D AF spin correlations develop rapidly from T*≈280 K to TN=266 K, coinciding with a large decrease in out-of-plane resistivity.
AI.motivation: To uncover the intrinsic magnetism and electrical conduction of the Cu-O plane in a cuprate that exhibits both antiferromagnetic (AF) and superconducting (SC) orders simultaneously.
AI.method: Examination of temperature and magnetic-field dependences of magnetization and electrical resistivity (including out-of-plane resistivity) in lightly-doped superconducting LCO single crystals (p≈0.03), compared with data from extremely lightly doped samples (p≲0.015).
AI.result: In SC LCO at p≈0.03, Cu sub-lattice moments and AF couplings are only ~15% smaller than in the Mott-insulator parent material, indicating strong localization of Cu 3d electrons. Two-dimensional AF spin correlations develop rapidly from T*≈280 K down to TN=266 K, where out-of-plane resistivity begins to decrease substantially.
AI.conclusion: The strong AF correlations and the rapid development of 2D spin fluctuations toward TN likely account for the persistence of AF ordering at high temperature (~266 K) even in a superconducting single-layer cuprate at p≈0.03.

title: Directional Hydrogen Migration in Acetonitrile Dication in Asymmetric Ultrashort Intense Laser Fields
summary: We investigate intramolecular hydrogen migration in acetonitrile dication in phase-controlled $ω$-$2ω$ intense laser fields (800 and 400 nm, 3.3$\times$10$^{14}$ W/cm$^2$) using three-dimensional coincidence ion momentum imaging. The two-body Coulomb explosion pathway, CH$_3$CN$^{2+}$ $\rightarrow$ CH$_3^+$ + CN$^+$, exhibits a clear phase-dependent fragment asymmetry along the laser polarization direction, showing that the tunnel ionization preferentially prepares the acetonitrile dication with the methyl group pointing toward the smaller amplitude side of the laser electric fields. The Coulomb explosion pathway occurring after the migration of a single hydrogen atom, CH$_3$CN$^{2+}$ $\rightarrow$ CH$_2^+$ + HCN$^+$, shows a pronounced reduction in the fragment asymmetry. A clear deuteration effect observed for the asymmetry of the hydrogen-migration pathway suggests that the two-color asymmetric laser field has a significant impact on directionality of intramolecular hydrogen migration in acetonitrile dication.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates intramolecular hydrogen migration in acetonitrile dication (CH3CN2+) using phase-controlled ω-2ω intense laser fields (800 and 400 nm, 3.3×10^14 W/cm^2) with three-dimensional coincidence ion momentum imaging. The direct Coulomb explosion pathway (CH3++CN+) shows clear phase-dependent fragment asymmetry, while the hydrogen-migration pathway (CH2++HCN+) exhibits reduced asymmetry and a deuteration effect, indicating that the two-color asymmetric laser field significantly controls the directionality of intramolecular hydrogen migration.
AI.motivation: To understand and control the directionality of intramolecular hydrogen migration in small polyatomic molecules using asymmetric two-color laser fields, which is relevant to controlling chemical reactions at the molecular level.
AI.method: Phase-controlled ω-2ω intense laser fields (800 and 400 nm) were used to ionize acetonitrile, and the resulting ion fragments were detected via three-dimensional coincidence ion momentum imaging to analyze Coulomb explosion pathways and fragment asymmetries.
AI.result: The direct Coulomb explosion pathway (CH3CN2+ → CH3+ + CN+) shows clear phase-dependent asymmetry along the laser polarization, with the methyl group preferentially pointing toward the smaller amplitude side of the laser field. The hydrogen-migration pathway (CH3CN2+ → CH2+ + HCN+) shows reduced asymmetry, and a clear deuteration effect confirms the two-color field significantly influences the directionality of hydrogen migration.
AI.conclusion: Phase-controlled two-color intense laser fields can selectively influence the directionality of intramolecular hydrogen migration in acetonitrile dication, providing a means to control this ultrafast molecular process.

title: Optical Voltage Profiling of 2D Semiconductors via Proximal Exciton Sensing
summary: High contact resistances in atomically thin semiconductors often mask intrinsic electrical transport properties, particularly at low carrier densities where exotic correlated states emerge. We introduce optical voltage profiling, a noninvasive wide-field technique that replaces local voltage probes with a proximal monolayer MoSe$_2$ exciton sensor. Isolated by thin hexagonal boron nitride, this sensor converts the target's local electrostatic potential into spatially resolved modulations of exciton reflectance. Through pixel-wise in situ calibration, these signals yield quantitative two-dimensional voltage maps of an actively biased semiconductor device. Using this method, we demonstrate the carrier-density-driven metal-insulator transition in bilayer MoSe$_2$ and obtain channel resistances below 1 k$Ω$ despite M$Ω$-scale two-terminal resistances in the metallic region. The optically derived resistance exhibits a metal-insulator crossover near the resistance quantum $h/e^2$, and the voltage maps and reconstructed local conductivity reveal pronounced spatial heterogeneity in both insulating and metallic regimes. Beyond resolving channel resistance under high contact-resistance conditions, the technique provides spatially resolved access to microscopic transport heterogeneity in functional van der Waals devices.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce optical voltage profiling, a noninvasive wide-field technique using a proximal monolayer MoSe2 exciton sensor to map local electrostatic potentials in biased 2D semiconductor devices. This method overcomes high contact resistance, enabling measurement of the metal-insulator transition in bilayer MoSe2, resolving channel resistances below 1 kΩ despite MΩ-scale two-terminal resistances, and revealing spatial transport heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: High contact resistances in atomically thin semiconductors obscure intrinsic electrical transport properties, especially at low carrier densities where correlated states emerge. Traditional local voltage probes cannot be directly applied to these fragile 2D systems, creating a need for a noninvasive way to measure local potentials and transport.
AI.method: The technique uses a monolayer MoSe2 exciton sensor isolated by thin hexagonal boron nitride, positioned proximally to the target device. The sensor converts local electrostatic potential into spatially resolved modulations of exciton reflectance. Pixel-wise in situ calibration converts these reflectance signals into quantitative two-dimensional voltage maps of an actively biased semiconductor device.
AI.result: The method revealed the carrier-density-driven metal-insulator transition in bilayer MoSe2, achieving channel resistances below 1 kΩ despite MΩ-scale two-terminal resistances in the metallic regime. The optically derived resistance showed a metal-insulator crossover near the resistance quantum h/e^2. Voltage maps and reconstructed local conductivity displayed pronounced spatial heterogeneity in both insulating and metallic regimes.
AI.conclusion: Optical voltage profiling provides spatially resolved access to microscopic transport heterogeneity in functional van der Waals devices, overcoming high contact-resistance limitations and enabling intrinsic transport characterization in atomically thin semiconductors.

title: Finite-temperature Green's function cluster expansion from thermofield doubles: Breakdown of the polaron picture
summary: We introduce a method, numerically exact in principle, for computing the momentum- and frequency-resolved single-particle Green's function of a polaron at finite temperature. The method, which we refer to as the finite-temperature Green's function cluster expansion, combines two ingredients: the generalized Green's function cluster expansion, a numerically exact extension of the momentum average family of methods that solves the polaron problem at zero temperature through a hierarchy of equations of motion for restricted phonon cloud configurations; and the thermofield double formalism, which maps the thermal trace onto a pure-state expectation value over a doubled Hilbert space. The resulting equations of motion have the same algebraic structure as those of the multi-boson zero-temperature theory, with the temperature entering through a Bogoliubov-type mixing angle that controls the coupling to a set of fictitious bath bosons. We implement the method in our open-source software package and benchmark it on the one-dimensional Holstein polaron, computing spectral functions, dispersions, lifetimes, and effective masses across coupling regimes and temperatures up to $T/Ω\sim 1$. Where finite-temperature density matrix renormalization group results are available, we find quantitative agreement at affordable computational cost. The method recovers momentum-resolved spectra directly in frequency space, with no time evolution or analytic continuation. We also discuss the practical costs of the approach. In particular, since the doubled phonon Hilbert space has a non-trivial configuration structure in which real and fictitious clouds compete, convergence in the corresponding cloud parameters requires care.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the finite-temperature Green's function cluster expansion, a numerically exact method for computing momentum- and frequency-resolved single-particle Green's functions of polarons at finite temperature. It combines the generalized Green's function cluster expansion (zero-temperature) with the thermofield double formalism, resulting in equations of motion with the same algebraic structure as the multi-boson zero-temperature theory plus Bogoliubov-type temperature mixing. The method is benchmarked on the 1D Holstein polaron, achieving quantitative agreement with DMRG results at affordable cost, directly in frequency space without analytic continuation.
AI.motivation: Polaron physics at finite temperature remains computationally challenging; existing methods for momentum-resolved spectral functions at finite temperature are limited by cost, the need for analytic continuation, or restricted parameter regimes. A numerically exact, direct-in-frequency-space method is needed.
AI.method: The method fuses the generalized Green's function cluster expansion (a numerically exact extension of momentum-average methods using a hierarchy of equations of motion for restricted phonon cloud configurations) with the thermofield double formalism, which maps the thermal trace onto a pure-state expectation value over a doubled Hilbert space. Temperature enters via a Bogoliubov-type mixing angle coupling to fictitious bath bosons, preserving the algebraic structure of the zero-temperature multi-boson equations of motion.
AI.result: Benchmarked on the 1D Holstein polaron across coupling regimes and temperatures up to T/Ω ~ 1, the method produces spectral functions, dispersions, lifetimes, and effective masses. Quantitative agreement with existing finite-temperature DMRG results is achieved at affordable computational cost, directly in frequency space without time evolution or analytic continuation.
AI.conclusion: The finite-temperature Green's function cluster expansion is a viable, accurate, and cost-effective approach for finite-temperature polaron spectral functions in the benchmarked regime. Practical limitations are discussed, notably that the doubled phonon Hilbert space has a non-trivial configuration structure (real and fictitious clouds compete), requiring careful convergence in cloud parameters.

title: Writing and erasing skyrmions by single ultrafast laser pulses in monolayer Janus 2D magnets
summary: Skyrmions in 2D magnets are promising candidates for nonvolatile, low-power, and high-density spintronic memories. However, their experimental realization at the 2D limit remains challenging, owing to the difficulty in engineering the required chiral magnetic interactions. Here, we report the creation and direct imaging of Néel-type skyrmions in Janus 2D chromium chalcogenides using synchrotron X-ray photoemission electron microscopy, and scanning nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry, which exhibit field-free stability, nonvolatility, and size tunability. First-principles calculations and micromagnetic simulations reveal that Janus-surface-induced inversion-symmetry breaking enhances the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, providing the microscopic mechanism for skyrmion stabilization and tunability. We further achieve reversible skyrmion writing and erasing using a single ultrafast laser pulse in a magnetic field as low as 300 Oe, demonstrating the excellent manipulability of this 2D magnetic system. These results establish Janus engineering as a route to creating and manipulating nonvolatile skyrmions in atomically thin magnets, with implications for skyrmion-based low-power spintronic devices.

AI.tldr: The authors create and directly image Néel-type skyrmions in Janus 2D chromium chalcogenides using synchrotron X-ray photoemission electron microscopy and scanning nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry, demonstrating field-free stability, nonvolatility, and size tunability. They achieve reversible single ultrafast-laser-pulse writing/erasing at low magnetic fields (300 Oe), with first-principles calculations revealing that Janus-surface-induced inversion-symmetry breaking enhances the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction as the stabilization mechanism.
AI.motivation: Skyrmions in 2D magnets are promising for nonvolatile, low-power, high-density spintronic memories, but their experimental realization at the 2D limit remains challenging due to the difficulty in engineering the required chiral magnetic interactions.
AI.method: The authors use synchrotron X-ray photoemission electron microscopy (X-PEEM) and scanning nitrogen-vacancy (NV) magnetometry for direct skyrmion imaging, combined with first-principles calculations and micromagnetic simulations. They also employ single ultrafast laser pulses for reversible skyrmion writing/erasing.
AI.result: Creation and direct imaging of Néel-type skyrmions in Janus 2D chromium chalcogenides with field-free stability, nonvolatility, and size tunability. Reversible skyrmion writing and erasing achieved with a single ultrafast laser pulse in a magnetic field as low as 300 Oe.
AI.conclusion: Janus engineering is established as a route to creating and manipulating nonvolatile skyrmions in atomically thin magnets, with implications for skyrmion-based low-power spintronic devices. Janus-surface-induced inversion-symmetry breaking enhances the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, providing the microscopic stabilization mechanism.

title: Universal Machine-learning Molecular Dynamics at the Speed of Empirical Potentials
summary: No interatomic potential has offered universality across chemistry, near-first-principles accuracy and the speed of empirical potentials at once. Here we introduce DPA4C, an equivariant potential whose architecture and compressed CUDA operators are co-designed under deployment constraints to pursue accuracy and efficiency together. Five variants spanning a 49-fold parameter range form the high-throughput end of the measured accuracy--throughput frontier. The largest variant approaches the accuracy of the MACE-Omat models at about two orders of magnitude higher measured throughput. The most compact reduces the energy, force and stress errors of the fastest existing universal MLIP by 61.4%, 48.1% and 34.3% at 1.92 times its saturated throughput. All five variants complete multimillion-atom simulations on a single GPU and run molecular dynamics for 2.048 billion atoms on 1,024 16-GB NVIDIA V100 GPUs at 83.3--91.2% weak-scaling efficiency. Compared with the MEAM empirical potential, DPA4C-Nano reaches 1.8 and 2.5 times the saturated throughput in single-GPU scans on the same V100 hardware for diamond carbon and FCC copper, respectively. DPA4C therefore brings quantum-trained universal accuracy into a regime of speed and system size previously associated with empirical potentials.

AI.tldr: DPA4C is an equivariant interatomic potential that co-designs its architecture and CUDA operators under deployment constraints, achieving near-first-principles accuracy at speeds approaching empirical potentials. Its five variants span a 49-fold parameter range, with the largest approaching MACE-Omat accuracy at ~100x higher throughput and the smallest improving error metrics by 34-61% over the fastest existing universal MLIP at 1.92x its saturated throughput. It scales to 2.048 billion atoms across 1,024 V100 GPUs with 83-91% weak-scaling efficiency.
AI.motivation: No existing interatomic potential simultaneously offers universality across chemistry, near-first-principles accuracy, and empirical-potential-level speed. The authors aim to close this gap by co-designing an equivariant potential's architecture and low-level CUDA operators under deployment constraints.
AI.method: DPA4C employs an equivariant neural network architecture whose design is co-optimized with compressed CUDA kernels, targeting both accuracy and throughput jointly. Five model variants are provided across a 49-fold parameter range to sample different accuracy-throughput trade-offs on the Pareto frontier.
AI.result: The largest DPA4C variant approaches MACE-Omat accuracy at ~100x higher measured throughput. The most compact variant cuts energy/force/stress errors of the fastest existing universal MLIP by 61.4%, 48.1%, and 34.3% respectively while running at 1.92x its saturated throughput. All variants run multimillion-atom simulations on a single GPU and achieve 83.3-91.2% weak-scaling efficiency on 2.048 billion atoms across 1,024 V100 GPUs. DPA4C-Nano also outperforms the MEAM empirical potential in throughput on diamond carbon and FCC copper by 1.8x and 2.5x, respectively.
AI.conclusion: DPA4C successfully brings quantum-trained universal accuracy into the speed and scale regime previously associated with empirical potentials, demonstrating that architecture-CUDA co-design can break the traditional accuracy-speed trade-off in machine-learned interatomic potentials.

title: Predicting critical temperature in quantum simulators for high-$T_c$ superconductivity: the matrix product state plus mean field approach
summary: Quantum simulation based on ultra cold atomic lattice gases is one of the most promising platforms to investigate high-$T_c$ superconductivity beyond the limited capabilities of quantum many body numerics on classical computers. Yet, despite enormous progress since the field's inception, realizing a high-$T_c$ superconducting state still remains out of reach. The present work lays the groundwork to purpose the recently proposed, and already partly realized, mixed-dimensional (mixD) models, towards this end. These systems offer the proven capability to realize very high pairing energies while retaining appreciable mobility of pairs. We specifically investigate the potential of 2D mixD-models with anisotropic tunneling, using the matrix product state plus mean field theory (MPS+MF) for fermions, and show that these models may enter a high-$T_c$ superconducting phase. These simulations in turn are based on a comprehensive characterization of the 1D mixD-systems, which are the sub-units of which the 2D system is comprized. In this, we cover the range of currently experimentally relevant system sizes, and establish practical heuristics to determine when finite\hyp size effects preclude the use of a 1D mixD-system to build the 2D ones.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes mixed-dimensional (mixD) models with anisotropic tunneling as a path toward realizing high-Tc superconductivity in ultra-cold atomic lattice gas quantum simulators. Using matrix product state plus mean field theory (MPS+MF) for fermions, it shows that 2D mixD models may enter a high-Tc superconducting phase, building on a comprehensive characterization of their 1D subunits and establishing heuristics for finite-size effects at experimentally relevant system sizes.
AI.motivation: Ultra-cold atomic lattice gases are promising platforms for studying high-Tc superconductivity beyond classical numerical capabilities, yet realizing a high-Tc superconducting state has remained out of reach despite decades of progress. This work aims to overcome this impasse by leveraging recently proposed mixed-dimensional (mixD) models, which offer high pairing energies while retaining appreciable pair mobility.
AI.method: The authors employ matrix product state plus mean field theory (MPS+MF) for fermionic systems. They investigate 2D mixD models with anisotropic tunneling, building on a comprehensive characterization of 1D mixD systems (the subunits composing the 2D system). They establish practical heuristics to determine when finite-size effects preclude using a 1D mixD system to build 2D counterparts at currently experimentally relevant sizes.
AI.result: The simulations demonstrate that 2D mixD models with anisotropic tunneling may enter a high-Tc superconducting phase. The work also provides a comprehensive characterization of 1D mixD systems and practical heuristics for determining when finite-size effects make 1D subunits unsuitable for constructing 2D systems at experimentally relevant system sizes.
AI.conclusion: Mixed-dimensional models with anisotropic tunneling constitute a viable route toward realizing high-Tc superconductivity in quantum simulation platforms. The MPS+MF approach validates the potential of these systems, and the established heuristics provide practical guidance for experimental implementations by clarifying the boundaries of finite-size viability for building 2D systems from 1D subunits.

title: Comparative study of nonperturbative electron-positron pair production by intense laser fields colliding with either bremsstrahlung $γ$-rays or relativistic ions
summary: It is well known that electron-positron pairs can be created in the strong-field environments formed by (i) a high-intensity laser field and a high-energy $γ$-photon (nonlinear Breit-Wheeler process) or (ii) a high-intensity laser field and a nuclear Coulomb field (nonlinear Bethe-Heitler process). Both of these processes are particularly interesting in the interaction regime where the laser field enters nonperturbatively. Various experimental collaborations are currently aiming at detecting for the first time the nonperturbative Breit-Wheeler process, by exploiting high-intensity laser pulses and $γ$-ray sources based on bremsstrahlung. In contrast, an experimental observation of the nonlinear, nonperturbative Bethe-Heitler process still lies further ahead in the future because its technical realization appears at present more challenging. Our comparative study shows, however, that the physical properties of the total rates for the processes (i) and (ii) can become remarkably similar when the parameters for the bremsstrahlung-driven nonperturbative Breit-Wheeler process are properly chosen. In this sense, the upcoming experiments on the nonlinear Breit-Wheeler process could also be used to closely ``simulate'' the currently hard to observe nonlinear Bethe-Heitler process.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comparative theoretical study of two strong-field QED processes—nonlinear Breit-Wheeler (electron-positron pair creation from a laser field and a high-energy gamma photon) and nonlinear Bethe-Heitler (pair creation from a laser field and a nuclear Coulomb field). The authors show that with appropriately chosen parameters for a bremsstrahlung-driven nonperturbative Breit-Wheeler experiment, the total rates of the two processes become remarkably similar, suggesting that upcoming Breit-Wheeler experiments could effectively "simulate" the currently more challenging to observe nonlinear Bethe-Heitler process.
AI.motivation: While nonperturbative Breit-Wheeler processes are on the verge of experimental detection using high-intensity lasers and bremsstrahlung-based gamma sources, the corresponding nonlinear Bethe-Heitler process remains experimentally inaccessible due to greater technical challenges. The authors seek to determine whether upcoming Breit-Wheeler experiments could serve as a proxy for studying the physics of the Bethe-Heitler process.
AI.method: The authors perform a comparative theoretical analysis of the total pair-creation rates for both the nonlinear Breit-Wheeler and nonlinear Bethe-Heitler processes in the nonperturbative interaction regime, identifying parameter conditions under which the two processes exhibit remarkably similar physical characteristics.
AI.result: The comparative study demonstrates that with proper parameter choices for the bremsstrahlung-driven nonperturbative Breit-Wheeler process, the total rates for the two processes become strikingly similar, enabling the harder-to-observe Bethe-Heitler process to be closely simulated by the experimentally more accessible Breit-Wheeler process.
AI.conclusion: Upcoming experiments on the nonlinear Breit-Wheeler process can be exploited to effectively simulate the nonlinear Bethe-Heitler process, providing an experimentally feasible pathway to study strong-field pair-creation physics that would otherwise remain out of reach in the near future.

title: Isolating the natural edges of bilayer graphene in gate-defined mesoscopic devices
summary: We introduce a graphite-gated architecture for bilayer graphene devices in which the active device is completely isolated from the natural graphene edges. Using a single patterned graphite-gate layer, we realize a fully electrostatically defined Hall-bar. Longitudinal and Hall measurements reveal mesoscopic transport features, including Hall-effect quenching and magnetoresistance peaks associated with boundary scattering. The dependence of the mesoscopic features on the carrierdensity shows that the effective channel width increases with the Fermi level and the electrostatic confinement at the gate-defined boundaries, and indicates that the carriers scatter at the electrostatic boundary. Raman spectroscopy and Kelvin probe force microscopy suggest that this boundary is disordered due to the used fabrication methods. Comparably, the quantum mobility in a fieldeffect transistor fabricated with the same architecture is not limited by boundary scattering and the visibility of quantum oscillations down to 4 mT suggests a record value of 2.5 x 10^6 cm2/Vs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a graphite-gated architecture for bilayer graphene devices where the active device is fully isolated from natural graphene edges. Using a patterned graphite-gate layer, they fabricate a fully electrostatic Hall-bar that exhibits mesoscopic transport features (Hall-effect quenching and magnetoresistance peaks from boundary scattering). Raman and KPFM reveal the electrostatic boundaries are disordered from fabrication. In a comparable FET, quantum mobility reaches 2.5 x 10^6 cm²/Vs with quantum oscillations visible down to 4 mT, indicating record mobility not limited by boundary scattering.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limitations imposed by natural graphene edges and physical boundary scattering in conventional devices, aiming to achieve cleaner electrostatic confinement and higher carrier mobility in bilayer graphene devices.
AI.method: A graphite-gated architecture where a single patterned graphite-gate layer defines the device electrostatically, completely isolating the active region from natural graphene edges to form a fully electrostatic Hall-bar. Characterization includes Hall/longitudinal transport measurements, Raman spectroscopy, and Kelvin probe force microscopy.
AI.result: Mesoscopic transport features (Hall-effect quenching and magnetoresistance peaks) are observed due to boundary scattering; the effective channel width grows with Fermi level. The boundaries are disordered per Raman/KPFM. In a matched FET, quantum oscillations are visible down to 4 mT with a record quantum mobility of 2.5 x 10^6 cm²/Vs, not limited by boundary scattering.
AI.conclusion: The graphite-gated, edge-isolated architecture enables ultraclean bilayer graphene devices with record quantum mobility, and the boundary scattering observed in the Hall-bar geometry can be attributed to disordered electrostatic boundaries induced by fabrication, providing a pathway toward higher-quality gate-defined graphene devices.

title: Rare-earth spin textures and a route to electronic inhomogeneity in $Pr_2Ir_2O_7$
summary:
The pyrochlore iridate $Pr_2Ir_2O_7$ remains metallic at low temperatures where its family members insulate. Recently, scanning tunneling spectroscopy experiments have revealed an inhomogeneous mixture of Kondo-screened and Kondo-destroyed regions when its surface is produced by cleaving at room temperature while it remains uniform when cleaved at low temperatures. title: A single design choice determines whether machine learning models of materials make physically impossible predictions
summary: Machine-learned models are replacing first-principles calculations across materials discovery, and physical symmetry is the central guarantee built into them. The debate over how much symmetry to hard-wire rather than learn has run on rotations, where a symmetry error is an approximation error. Some constraints are exact: symmetry forces certain property tensors to exactly zero, so a nonzero prediction is physically impossible rather than inaccurate. Here we show that whether a model can make such predictions is decided before training by one rarely reported design bit, whether its features carry parity labels, and derive a criterion, the parity gap, that computes from group theory alone which properties and crystals are exposed. Across matched architecture pairs differing only in that bit, evaluated on two thousand centrosymmetric crystals whose piezoelectric tensor must vanish, parity-labelled arms sit at the floating-point floor while rotation-only arms predict forbidden responses on 90-96% of crystals, six orders of magnitude apart, at no accuracy cost. Training on explicit zeros does not recover exactness, and a head on a frozen universal potential inherits its backbone's symmetry group. One reflection at random initialization verifies the label in seconds.
